attacks.claim: The cost math mixes daily and monthly figures. The volumes are per day, so 2.28B tokens at $0.50/1M is about $1,140 per day, roughly $34K per month. That is about 23x the $1,500 budget, yet the plan labels the figure monthly and says it is within budget.
attacks.evidence: "Application logs: 38M lines/day average"; "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140"; "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: No spend controls exist, and prompt overhead and peak days are not costed. The 61M-line peak day and the fixed prompt resent on 8,640 calls per day are both omitted. There is no cap, sampling or budget alarm, so spend can run away.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: prompt token count, peak-day costing, spend cap or budget alarm

attacks.claim: Each 5-minute window is sent whole with no size limit. The average window is about 38M/8,640 ≈ 4,400 lines ≈ 264K tokens, which likely exceeds model context limits. Log storms during incidents will be far larger, so the design fails when summaries matter most.
attacks.evidence: "sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt"; ABSENT: per-window token cap, sampling or pre-aggregation

attacks.claim: The schedule is infeasible under the team charter. On-call work averages 50% of both engineers' time, so real capacity is about 6 eng-weeks. The plan budgets 12 eng-weeks of full-time work with no slack or descoping.
attacks.evidence: "on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time" vs "both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)"

attacks.claim: log-tap attaches to the production Vector pipeline with no isolation or backpressure design. Slowness in the queue or summarizer could delay or drop the logs responders rely on. There are also no timeouts, retries, rate-limit handling or lag alerts, and a failing summarizer would go unnoticed.
attacks.evidence: "forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue"; ABSENT: backpressure, timeouts, retries, alerting on summarizer lag

attacks.claim: The MTTR target (47 to 30 min) and the claim that the first 15-20 minutes go to grepping are unsupported. There is no baseline breakdown or prototype. Summary usefulness is only tested at the end, in week 6 or later.
attacks.evidence: "Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min"; "first 15-20 minutes grepping logs"

attacks.claim: Redaction covers only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs. Names, customer IDs and free-text personal data are not masked, and the Q1 audit covered the retention policy rather than export to an external LLM. A DPA and zero-retention reduce this risk.
attacks.evidence: "masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)"

attacks.claim: Log content is untrusted input to the LLM, and the output, including the 'suspected deploy' field, is posted into PagerDuty. No prompt-injection or output handling is described. Summaries are advisory only, which limits the impact.
attacks.evidence: "suspected deploy"; ABSENT: injection defense or output validation

attacks.claim: The 'within seconds of a page' goal is met only with staleness. The latest summary can be up to 5 minutes old, so it may miss the onset of the incident.
attacks.evidence: "within seconds of a page" vs "every 5 minutes"

attacks.claim: There is no kill switch or feature flag for the log-tap or the PagerDuty auto-comment.
The design depends on a single LLM vendor with no abstraction, fallback or data-region statement.
The eval is weakly valid. Incident commanders grade with hindsight of the outcome, and the logs for the 40 past incidents may be past retention.
attacks.evidence: "have the incident commander grade it"; ABSENT: blinding, retention check
